https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c151.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ukraine has developed drones, picture here in July 2026, capable of striking deep inside Russia By Ben Hatton Published 4 August 2026, 08:20 BST Updated 47 minutes ago At least five people were killed and 10 more injured in a Ukrainian drone strike on a warehouse close to Moscow overnight on Tuesday, the region's governor has said. The official did not specify what had been targeted but Ukraine has been carrying out strikes on facilities operated by Wildberries in recent weeks, often dubbed the "Russian Amazon". Kyiv says the depots are used to supply the Russian military, which Moscow denies. Local officials also said Wildberries warehouses were targeted in the St Petersburg and Tver regions overnight. Russia also launched strikes against parts of Ukraine, killing at least four and injuring several people. Russia's defence ministry said it had intercepted and destroyed 320 drones overnight. Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said an industrial site in Novoselki, Chekhov - about 69km (43 miles) south of the Kremlin - was attacked, triggering a fire at a warehouse. He wrote on Telegram that seven of the 10 people injured were in a moderate condition, with one in a serious condition. Ukrainian media reported that the site of the Moscow strike was linked to Wildberries. The company has not commented publicly but confirmed its facility in St Petersburg was hit. Meanwhile, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said an 89-year-old woman was killed and two girls, aged two and 12, were among seven injured in a Russian strike on the southern port city of Mykolaiv overnight. A woman and two girls, aged five and 10, were killed in a strike on a residential area in Sumy, and another four people were injured, it said. Russian strikes also injured two people in the city of Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, while a food warehouse was set on fire in Dnipro, according to the State Emergency Service. Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian Mexico Strangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’ With plentiful jobs and community support, one Mexico City neighbourhood has become a haven for those who have lived much of their lives in the US Oscar Lopez in Mexico City Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W ith its wide avenues lined with tall palm trees, its quaint cafes and old-school cantinas, as well as the mix of English and Spanish spoken on the street, the Tabacalera neighborhood in downtown Mexico City has a certain US feel – so much so that it is has become known as Little LA . The nickname is about more than appearances, however. In recent years, this corner of the metropolis has become a haven for many Mexicans deported from the US, particularly those who spent years or decades living across the border and for whom Mexico feels like a foreign country. In Little LA, they have found a more familiar place to belong. With the Trump administration embarking on a massive anti-immigrant crackdown, deportations to Mexico are expected to surge. Since taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump has deported roughly 145,500 Mexican nationals. Christopher Gil Ortíz was one of them. He was on his way to work in Los Angeles in June this year when Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents stopped him, handcuffed him and threw him in detention. View image in fullscreen Anti-Trump graffiti in the Tabacalera neighborhood. Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian After months of living in constant fear as an undocumented immigrant in Trump’s US, Ortíz said that when the detention finally happened he felt relieved. “At this point I was like, OK, that’s it, I’m going back,” he recalled. “It’s like they took a weight off my shoulders.” More than 30 years since he had left as a child, Ortíz was sent back to Mexico, leaving behind his wife and two young children. Dumped in the resort town of Tulum, he made his way to Cancún, only to have all his belongings stolen from his hotel room. Eventually, he ended up in Mexico City, where he had family. “I was nervous,” he said. “Even though I was born here, I have very vague memories of the city itself.” He was also facing the many challenges of being a deportee: getting his birth certificate, ID and finding a job. His sister sent him a TikTok post from an organization called New Comienzos (New Beginnings). Based in Little LA, it was set up to help returnees reintegrate. When he saw the post, Ortiz decided to check out Little LA for himself. View image in fullscreen Christopher Gil Ortíz, who was sent back to Mexico more than 30 years after he left as a child. Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian “Seeing the palm trees, it kind of does make you feel like you’re in LA,” he said, adding that he was grateful to New Comienzos. “There’s a lot of people that are going through what I’m going through and I’m pretty sure there’s going to be more.” The New Comienzos founder and executive director, Israel Concha, said he was preparing for exactly that. “The atmosphere [in the US] right now is one of humanitarian crisis and panic. People no longer even want to take their children to school,” Concha said. “You’ll probably start seeing mass deportations in a few months.” Concha founded New Comienzos when he witnessed first-hand how little support the Mexican government was offering recent arrivals. In 2012, he was living in Texas with his pregnant wife and had started a successful private transport business. He had lived in the US for 30 years. “I wanted to try to achieve that American dream, and I think I succeeded,” he said. View image in fullscreen In Little LA, many of those sent back from the US have found a more familiar place to belong. Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian Then one day he was caught speeding on his way to pick up a client. While in detention, he fought his case for two years but was deported in 2014. On his first day in Mexico, he was kidnapped by a criminal gang working with local police. “That was my welcome to my native country,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Thing Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The ‘self-deportee’ hounded out of the US to Mexico: ‘There are days when I feel literally insane’ Read more After being severely beaten, Concha escaped to Mexico City, where he found a job at a bilingual call centre – one of several starting to pop up in the Tabacalera neighborhood, attracting young returnees who spoke fluent English. Less than a year later, he started New Comienzos to address the challenges faced by people like himself. “People didn’t just need a job; many of them needed emotional support because they had just lost everything following a deportation,” he said. The organisation offers legal support and free English certification and classes, as well as mentorship for recent arrivals. Little LA remains the organization’s center of operations. “A community reintegration lab,” said Concha, “that’s what we’ve created there in Little Los Angeles.” Sergio Aaron Pérez, 36, said the area felt like home. Wearing a Los Angeles Lakers jersey and baseball cap, his face and arms covered in tattoos, Pérez looked as though he had just stepped off the plane from the US. In fact, having lived in the US for more than 30 years, the former California resident was deported in 2011 for doing what he calls “bad things”. View image in fullscreen Sergio Aaron Pérez in Little LA. Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian In Little LA, he found work at call centers. “If you speak English there’s a lot of money,” said Pérez. “I love my city. There’s a lot of community.” Ortíz, for his part, had little interest in a call center job. He has applied for a job at a glass-making factory – work he used to do in the US. Next on his agenda: bringing his wife and children to Mexico. “My kids are OK with it,” he said. Referencing a local Mexican custom, he added: “My daughter told me that she was already practising drinking soda out of a plastic bag.” Explore more on these topics Mexico ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Donald Trump Trump administration US immigration Migration US politics features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Renee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help search Missing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of Nepal Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Cait Kelly in Kathmandu Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.21 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Clair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations. “Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them. “And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.” View image in fullscreen Renee, an Australian, was travelling in Nepal and is now missing. Photograph: GoFundMe Like many of the missing Australians , Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away. Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s. Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said. “And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.” A map showing the flood zone in Nepal Renee’s family understand how dire the situation is , and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived. But until they know for certain, they would hold hope, she said. “Everyone’s very realistic. We know how bad this was and where she was. But until they find her, everyone’s got this little slither of hope that maybe she’s stuck somewhere and can’t get out, or she’s injured. Families balance hope and despair in race to find survivors in Nepal as 41 Australians still missing Read more “I’ve been looking through pictures trying to identify someone or see her. But we understand the reality of this situation.” Like most Australians, Renee had come to Nepal on a pilgrimage. Spry said her sister was a “deeply spiritual” person who loved to help people. “She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” she said. “Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.” The family of Michael Keats, an Australian who had been near the Tibet-Nepal border when flash flooding began, confirmed his death in posts to social media on Sunday. Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram he had been on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash that had been a “dream for many years”. “Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said. “There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted then to know God, and to merge with the divine. ”He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: 9News Victoria Manhunt after alleged axe attack in Victoria leaves three people with serious injuries Police search for alleged attacker, in his 50s, after incident in Gippsland town of Tyers Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Sat 5 Sep 2026 20.22 EDT First published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 20.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three people have been taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries after an alleged axe attack in Victoria , with police still searching for the suspect. The alleged attacker, who is known to the victims, came to an address in the Gippsland town of Tyers at about 12.30pm on Saturday, according to a spokesperson for Victoria police. He is believed to have attacked an elderly man and woman, and a third person with an axe, causing serious injuries. The man, who is in his 50s, fled the address and the victims were able to call emergency services for help, police said. A specialist air ambulance and road paramedics were dispatched to the scene and all three victims were treated at the scene. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email A spokesperson for Ambulance Victoria said a man in his 70s and a man in his 40s were transported to hospital in a critical condition. A woman in her 70s was transported to hospital in a serious but stable condition, the spokesperson said. The man is believed to have left the property on foot. Victoria police launched a large-scale search for the man yesterday and were continuing to look for him on Sunday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The man was last seen wearing a black and mustard coloured jacket and carrying a black backpack, police said. Police warned he may be armed with an axe and handsaw. Police urged anyone who sees the offender to not approach the man and immediately contact Triple Zero (000). https://www.dw.com/en/us-award-winning-k.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NwE2 Friends and relatives say Arfat Sheikh's detention by ICE agents is 'unlawful' and are calling for his release [FILE: May 26, 2026] Image: Charly Triballeau/AFP Advertisement A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally. Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance." Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family. Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum. The DHS said Sheikh would receive due process but that a pending ​application does not confer legal residency status. ICE arrests up amid Trump immigration crackdown US President Donald Trump has been pursuing an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he claims is aimed at improving domestic security. His administration said in August it was to "identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently." The number of ICE arrests hit record levels this summer, with about 51,000 recorded across August. Critics say the crackdown has violated due process and ​free speech rights and ​has created an unsafe ⁠environment , particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling. ICE targets South Asians for removal from United States To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025. His first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, ​the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the ​Wake Forest ⁠Film Festival. The film explored conflict in Kashmir , a disputed Muslim-majority region claimed by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan , which each control only part of it and have fought wars over it.
